lesson.title: Integers: Whole Numbers and Their Mirror Images
lesson.summary: Integers extend the counting numbers in both directions, giving algebra a clean way to represent gains, losses, and everything in between.
lesson.body:
Integers are the whole numbers and their opposites: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, .... They extend the counting numbers you first learned in both directions, giving you a way to represent quantities that go below zero, such as a temperature of -10 degrees, an elevation of -50 feet below sea level, or a debt of 20 dollars written as -20. Integers contain no fractions or decimals; every integer is a complete, unbroken unit. This set matters because many real situations, gains and losses, deposits and withdrawals, cannot be described honestly using only positive counting numbers.

Integers are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication, which means adding, subtracting, or multiplying any two integers always produces another integer. For example, 5 + (-8) = -3, an integer; 4 - 9 = -5, an integer; and (-6)(3) = -18, an integer. Division is the exception: dividing two integers does not always give an integer, since 7 divided by 2 equals 3.5, which is not a whole number. This gap is exactly why the number system needs to grow further, into the rational numbers, to handle division cleanly.

Adding and subtracting integers follows predictable sign rules. When signs match, add the absolute values and keep the shared sign: -4 + (-7) = -11. When signs differ, subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger and keep the sign of the number with the larger absolute value: -9 + 5 = -4, because 9 is larger than 5 and negative wins. Subtraction can always be rewritten as adding the additive inverse: 6 - 10 becomes 6 + (-10) = -4, using the same inverse property covered earlier.

Worked example: a submarine starts at a depth of -120 feet relative to sea level. It rises 45 feet, then descends 30 feet. Find its final depth. Rising is adding a positive integer, and descending is adding a negative integer, so compute -120 + 45 + (-30). First, -120 + 45 = -75. Then, -75 + (-30) = -105. The submarine ends at -105 feet, meaning 105 feet below sea level. Every step used only integer arithmetic, and the answer is itself an integer, consistent with closure under addition.

Multiplying integers follows its own sign rule: a positive times a positive, or a negative times a negative, gives a positive product, while a positive times a negative gives a negative product. For example, (-3)(-4) = 12, but (-3)(4) = -12. This pattern extends to more factors: multiplying three negative integers gives a negative result, since the first two negatives cancel to a positive, and that positive times the third negative becomes negative again, as in (-2)(-3)(-5) = 6 * (-5) = -30. Counting how many negative factors are present, an even count gives a positive result, an odd count gives a negative result, is a fast way to predict the sign before multiplying everything out.

Integers build on the idea of Number by formally including negative values and zero alongside the positive counting numbers. This concept is foundational for nearly everything that follows: the number line needs integers as evenly spaced landmarks, exponent rules rely on integer exponents, and rational numbers are literally built as ratios of integers. Getting comfortable with integer sign rules now pays off every time a negative number shows up later in the course.
